crime.value: No conventional crime; the central puzzle is a supernatural encounter — an apparently long-dead Yuma Territorial Prison convict digs a hole in a new freeway and finds water. Question: was the old man real, and how did the pavement come to be chipped open and filled with water?
crime.quote: The barricades were a neat fence, framing a large chipped hole in the freeway.

victim.value: Arguably the old prospector-convict himself: a man imprisoned in the 'caves'/'bake ovens' of Yuma Territorial Prison, who died unrested longing for his water hole
victim.quote: “Nobody’s goin’ to shut me up in that filth again. Them caves. Bake ovens.”

closed_world.value: An isolated stretch of new freeway across empty Arizona desert between Gila Bend and Yuma, with only Harry, Myra, and the old man present
closed_world.quote: “There’s only the next town of Gila Bend, and then it’s all empty desert.”

culprit_and_motive.value: The ghost of the old prisoner/prospector, driven by his unfinished compulsion to find his water hole so he can rest
culprit_and_motive.quote: “I gotta find my water hole. My own good pure water from my own water hole.”

resolution.value: No investigative solution; confirmation instead — the water-filled hole, the damp rusty pick, and the permanent gouge in the fender prove the encounter was real
resolution.quote: cannot seem to straighten out the sharp narrow gouge in the center of the left rear fender

investigator.value: Myra, the wife and first-person narrator, an ordinary witness recounting the event; her husband Harry supplies the deductive guess about the prison
investigator.quote: “It points the way to the Territorial Prison. I think we’d just better stop off there and tell the authorities”

suspect_architecture.value: Not a whodunit cast; effectively one enigmatic figure — the ragged old prospector encountered on the freeway — with Myra and Harry as the only other participants. Differentiation is between Myra (believes, compassionate) and Harry (skeptical, protective).
suspect_architecture.quote: "He's just a tired old man, Harry," I whispered. "He must have walked miles."

red_herring.value: The rational explanation planted repeatedly: that the old man is a living escaped convict from Yuma Territorial Prison, sun-maddened — leading the couple (and reader) to a police-report resolution rather than the supernatural one.
red_herring.quote: "You think he was an escaped prisoner?" I asked.

clue_fairness.value: Clues are shown to the reader as the narrator sees them: Harry's failure to see the man, the man's dread of Yuma and talk of caves/bake ovens, blood-red manacle-burned wrists, the pick striking the fender — all precede the revelation.
clue_fairness.quote: "Ain't from Yuma," the voice was defiant. "Ain't never been to Yuma. Never. Whole life."

social_world.value: Mid-century American middle-class domesticity — travelling salesman husband, wife of three teen daughters, deference to male authority — set against frontier/territorial history and the institutional cruelty of the Yuma prison system.
social_world.quote: Like one of the girls, having to take an order without explanation, I obeyed my husband.

alibi.value: The old man's denial of any connection to Yuma functions as a false alibi, immediately undercut by his own description of the prison's caves and ovens.
alibi.quote: "Nobody's goin' to shut me up in that filth again. Them caves. Bake ovens."

reveal_mechanic.value: Physical residue proving the encounter was real yet impossible: the freshly chipped hole in new pavement brimming with water, the ancient rusty pick damp at the edge, and the unfixable gouge in the station wagon's fender.
reveal_mechanic.quote: cannot seem to straighten out the sharp narrow gouge in the center of the left rear fender

media_and_audience.value: Experience filtered through television Western imagery and the prison-turned-museum's packaging of history as tourist spectacle; the narrator frames her account defensively for a disbelieving audience.
media_and_audience.quote: It was every television Western, every sheriff who fought to get the prisoner to the Territorial Prison

investigator_wound.value: Myra's loneliness and guilt over a marriage thinned by Harry's constant travel; the case destroys her trust in rational explanation and leaves her sleepless and dream-haunted when he is away.
investigator_wound.quote: I'm not much good with Harry away any more... I get nervous and have strange dreams.

suspect_wounds.value: Myra's only 'suspect' status is internal — she alone sees the old man, making her look hysterical or 'berserk' to her husband; Harry's guilt at not seeing the man drives his behavior.
suspect_wounds.quote: "Isn't it enough," he said fiercely, "that you go suddenly berserk and get us into this fix without—"

unreliable_frame.value: Myra narrates in first person and opens by explicitly disclaiming her own credibility, inviting the reader to disbelieve her account of the encounter.
unreliable_frame.quote: I’m not asking you to believe it, you understand. In a way, I don’t even want you to.

setting_as_constraint.value: The empty Arizona desert freeway between Gila Bend and Yuma — soft sand shoulders, no towns for hours, sealed air-conditioned car — isolates the couple so no witness or help exists.
setting_as_constraint.quote: There’s only the next town of Gila Bend, and then it’s all empty desert.

evidence_type.value: Physical/environmental residue: the rusty ancient pick damp with water, the freshly chipped water-filled hole in new pavement, and the ineradicable gouge in the car's fender.
evidence_type.quote: the best mechanics in town, or in the city, cannot seem to straighten out the sharp narrow gouge

false_suspect.value: The old prospector is taken for an escaped convict from Yuma Territorial Prison; Harry intends to report him, only to learn the prison has been a ruin and museum for a century.
false_suspect.quote: “You think he was an escaped prisoner?” I asked.

technical_detail.value: Local Arizona history — Yuma Territorial Prison (1825), its rock-cut 'cave' cells and manacle rings, now a museum — decodes the old man's ravings about caves, ovens and filth.

moral_ambiguity.value: The threatening old man is not malevolent but a tormented soul, imprisoned and baked in stone cells, whose violence stems from terror of being returned and an unappeasable thirst.
moral_ambiguity.quote: “Nobody’s goin’ to shut me up in that filth again. Them caves. Bake ovens.”
